Control Systems Engineering Laboratory • Parametric Tuning & Benchmark Study

Experimental STSMC Gain Optimization & Multi-Profile Benchmark

Systematic 30-Trial Simulation Study Across 6 Road Profiles & Continuous Future RSI Scope
Course: Control Systems
Program: B.Tech Electrical and Computer Science
Authors: Thilang T.V (25BEL0036), Santhosh G (25BEL0016), Ananthakrishnan R (25BEL0005)
Platform: Quanser 2-DOF Active Suspension (QC-ASSM)
Environment: MATLAB / Simulink 2025b (ODE45 FastRestart)
Total Simulation Trials: 30 Empirical Runs + 21 Continuous RSI Points

1. Executive Summary & Physics of the Pareto Trade-off

This investigation executes a comprehensive, empirical parameter sweep and multi-profile comparative study of the Super-Twisting Sliding Mode Controller (STSMC) applied to the Quanser 2-DOF Quarter-Car Active Suspension System Model (QC-ASSM). To address the fundamental trade-off between passenger ride comfort (minimizing sprung mass vertical acceleration z̈s) and mechanical rattle space limitations (constraining suspension stroke zs - zus within the physical ± 38.0 mm limit), five distinct parameter configurations (c1, k1, k2) were evaluated across all six standardized road disturbance profiles:

  • Candidate 1 (Low Gains / Soft Compliance): Designed for minimal control effort and soft ride, but risks large suspension stroke excursions under severe excitation.
  • Candidate 2 (Standard Grant Proposal Baseline): The original fixed parameter table proposed in the initial grant specifications.
  • Candidate 3 (Fixed STSMC Baseline Reference): The un-adapted robust STSMC baseline (c1 = 7.0, k1 = 60.0, k2 = 25.0).
  • Candidate 4 (Aggressive Tuning / Iteration 1): Over-stiffened gains (k1 up to 180, c1 up to 15) that aggressively restrict stroke but increase body acceleration.
  • Candidate 5 (Precision Tuned / Iteration 2 Optimal): Monotonically scheduled parameters synthesized in stsmc_rsi_scheduler.m that achieve the global optimum across 100% of the profiles.
Figure 1: Parallel Simulink Benchmark Architecture (Master_Active_Suspension.slx) showing Lane 1 (Optimal LQR), Lane 2 (Fixed STSMC), Lane 3 (Adaptive STSMC), Comparison Scopes, and In-Simulink RMS Digital Displays.

2. Mathematical Formulation & Root-Cause Diagnosis

The continuous-time state-space dynamics of the 2-DOF Quanser Quarter-Car model are governed by:

ẋ(t) = A x(t) + B uin(t),   x = [zs - zus,   żs,   zus - zr,   żus]T,   uin = [żr,   uc]T

The Super-Twisting Sliding Mode Control law synthesizes a continuous control signal by integrating the signum operator, effectively attenuating high-frequency chattering without actuator wear:

s(t) = c1 (zs - zus) + żs
uc(t) = -k1 √|s(t)| tanh(s(t) / εsmc) + v(t),   v̇(t) = -k2 tanh(s(t) / εsmc)
usat(t) = clip(uc(t), -39.2 N, +39.2 N),   εsmc = 0.010
Diagnostic Resolution: The Physics of High RMS Acceleration in Iteration 1
The sprung mass acceleration equation is given by:
z̈s = (1 / ms) [ -ks (zs - zus) - bs (żs - żus) + uc(t) ]
In Iteration 1, excessive gains (k1 = 160–180, c1 = 14–15) caused the linear DC actuator to generate large instantaneous counter-forces (peaking > 21 N) in an attempt to drive the sliding variable s(t) to zero. While this restricted suspension deflection to 17.95 mm, the excessive control force uc acted directly on the chassis, elevating steady-state RMS acceleration above the Fixed STSMC baseline. By moderating the gains in Iteration 2 (k1 ≤ 78, c1 ≤ 8.0), the suspension is allowed sufficient compliance (deflection ∼ 21.5 mm, well within the 38 mm limit) to absorb high-frequency road energy, cutting steady-state RMS acceleration below both Fixed STSMC and LQR.

4. Detailed Sensitivity Curves & Pareto Trade-Off Analysis by Road Profile

For each profile, the 4-panel analysis displays: (1) Steady-state RMS Acceleration across candidates, (2) Peak suspension travel against the ± 38.0 mm limit, (3) Peak actuator force against the ± 39.2 N motor limit, and (4) The Comfort vs. Rattle Space Pareto frontier.

Profile 1: Smooth road (Severity RSI = 0.10)

Engineering Rationale: On smooth surfaces, disturbance forces are negligible. Low sliding manifold slope (c1=5.0) and moderate proportional gains (k1=20) prioritize vehicle chassis vibration isolation without inducing unnecessary actuator counter-forces.

Figure 2: Parameter tuning sensitivity, hardware constraint compliance, and Pareto frontier for Profile 1 (Smooth road).

Profile 2: Normal road (Severity RSI = 0.25)

Engineering Rationale: Resonance excitation causes vehicle body bounce amplification. Under-damped gains (Grant table k1=18) result in resonance excursion (SS RMS 3.13 m/s²). Aggressive gains (k1=120) over-stiffen the suspension (SS RMS 1.27 m/s²). Precision tuning (c1=6.5, k1=55, k2=22) achieves optimal damping balance at 1.0869 m/s².

Figure 3: Parameter tuning sensitivity, hardware constraint compliance, and Pareto frontier for Profile 2 (Normal road).

Profile 3: Rough road (Severity RSI = 0.40)

Engineering Rationale: Broadband chirp sweeps pass through resonance at 3 Hz and tire hop at 8 Hz. Precision tuning (c1=6.8, k1=62, k2=25) minimizes steady-state RMS acceleration (4.1471 m/s²) while keeping stroke well within limits (18.47 mm).

Figure 4: Parameter tuning sensitivity, hardware constraint compliance, and Pareto frontier for Profile 3 (Rough road).

Profile 4: Bumpy road (Severity RSI = 0.55)

Engineering Rationale: Transient ramp impacts require gentle compliant initial entry followed by controlled settling. Precision tuning (c1=5.8, k1=45, k2=18) absorbs the 20 mm bump with 5.73 mm stroke and minimal body acceleration (0.0979 m/s²).

Figure 5: Parameter tuning sensitivity, hardware constraint compliance, and Pareto frontier for Profile 4 (Bumpy road).

Profile 5: Pulse road (Severity RSI = 0.70)

Engineering Rationale: Step drops impose high initial impact shocks. While aggressive gains clamp deflection to 18.17 mm, they transfer excessive jerk to the body (1.0117 m/s²). Precision tuning (c1=7.8, k1=75, k2=30) achieves 0.8282 m/s² with 40.8% stroke safety margin (22.51 mm).

Figure 6: Parameter tuning sensitivity, hardware constraint compliance, and Pareto frontier for Profile 5 (Pulse road).

Profile 6: Potholes road (Severity RSI = 0.85)

Engineering Rationale: Pothole strikes threaten mechanical bottoming. Precision tuning (c1=8.0, k1=78, k2=32) ensures robust bump-stop clearance (21.50 mm vs. 38.0 mm limit) while delivering the lowest steady-state RMS acceleration (1.2316 m/s²).

Figure 7: Parameter tuning sensitivity, hardware constraint compliance, and Pareto frontier for Profile 6 (Potholes road).

5. Continuous RSI Gain Scheduling Curve (Future Road Profile Scope)

To equip the active suspension system for arbitrary future road disturbances (e.g. washboard gravel, cobblestone, bridge expansion joints) detected via real-time Edge AI vision, stsmc_rsi_scheduler.m implements a continuous, piecewise-monotonic 8-node interpolation function across the entire domain RSI ∈ [0.0, 1.0].

6. Key Technical Conclusions & Engineering Sign-Off

  1. Superiority of Precision-Tuned STSMC (Candidate 5): Achieves the lowest steady-state RMS acceleration across 100% of the 6 test profiles, beating Optimal LQR, Fixed STSMC, and all other candidate sets.
  2. Full Hardware Safety Compliance: Maximum suspension stroke across all 30 simulation runs was 22.51 mm, providing a 40.8% safety buffer from the ± 38.0 mm hard stops. Maximum actuator force was 20.38 N, preserving a 48.0% buffer from the ± 39.2 N motor saturation limit.
  3. Strict Monotonicity for Edge AI Vision Scope: The 8-node piecewise linear continuous scheduling function guarantees that as road severity increases from 0.0 to 1.0, controller gains scale smoothly without numerical chatter, instability, or chattering.
  4. Zero Numerical Artifacts: Clamping the continuous RMS integrator saturation limit to 0 permanently eliminated complex square root warnings during simulation.
